claims.text: Before starting: get consent and check the patient's wristband, the unit label and the compatibility report at the bedside
claims.quote: Before transfusion is started, consent should be obtained, and the patient’s wristband, blood unit label, and compatibility test report must be checked at the bedside to ensure that the blood component is the one intended for the recipient.

claims.text: ABO: as a rule give the recipient's own ABO type; when the type is unknown or in doubt in an urgent situation, type O Rh-negative packed RBCs (not whole blood) can go to any ABO type
claims.quote: As a rule, blood for transfusion should be of the same ABO type as that of the recipient. In urgent situations or when the correct ABO type is in doubt or unknown, type O Rh-negative packed RBCs (not whole blood—see Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction), which contains neither A nor B antigens, may be used for patients of any ABO type.

claims.text: Rh: Rh-negative patients always get Rh-negative blood unless it is unavailable in a life-threatening emergency; Rh-positive patients may get either
claims.quote: Rh-negative patients should always receive Rh-negative blood except in life-threatening emergencies when Rh-negative blood is unavailable. Rh-positive patients may receive Rh-positive or Rh-negative blood.

claims.text: Emergency transfusion (generally < 60 minutes to test): ABO/Rh type-specific blood needs about 10 minutes; with the type unknown, give type O RBCs, Rh-negative for females of child-bearing age if Rh is also unknown
claims.quote: Emergency transfusion is done when not enough time (generally < 60 minutes) is available for thorough compatibility testing because the patient is in hemorrhagic shock. When time permits (approximately 10 minutes is needed), ABO/Rh type-specific blood may be given. In urgent situations when the patient’s blood type is unknown, type O RBCs are transfused. If Rh status is also unknown, Rh-negative blood is used for females of child-bearing age to prevent alloimmunization; in other patients, either Rh-negative or Rh-positive type O blood may be given.

claims.text: Type and screen: ABO/Rh typing plus an antibody screen, for cases unlikely to need blood (e.g., low-bleeding-risk surgery)
claims.quote: “Type and screen” may be requested in circumstances that are not likely to require transfusion, as in surgery in which the risk of bleeding is low. The patient’s blood is typed for ABO/Rh antigens and screened for antibodies.

claims.text: Most common signs of a reaction: chills, rigors, fever, dyspnea, light-headedness, urticaria, itching, flank pain
claims.quote: The most common symptoms of transfusion reactions are chills, rigor, fever, dyspnea, light-headedness, urticaria, itching, and flank pain.

claims.text: Any of these (except localized urticaria and itching): stop the transfusion at once, keep the IV line open with normal saline, and send the rest of the unit plus clotted and anticoagulated patient blood samples to the blood bank
claims.quote: If any of these symptoms (other than localized urticaria and itching) occur, the transfusion should be stopped immediately and the IV line kept open with normal saline. The remainder of the blood product and clotted and anticoagulated samples of the patient’s blood should be sent to the blood bank for investigation.

claims.text: After a reaction: don't restart that unit or start any previously issued unit; hold further transfusion until the cause is known, and if blood is urgent use type O Rh-negative RBCs
claims.quote: NOTE: The unit in question should not be restarted, and transfusion of any previously issued unit should not be initiated. Further transfusion should be delayed until the cause of the reaction is known, unless the need is urgent, in which case type O Rh-negative red blood cells (RBCs) should be used.

claims.text: Hemolytic reactions: acute (within 24 hours) or delayed (1 to 14 days)
claims.quote: Hemolytic reactions may be acute (within 24 hours) or delayed (from 1 to 14 days).

claims.text: Febrile reaction: temperature rise of ≥ 1° C with chills, sometimes headache and back pain; because fever and chills also herald a hemolytic reaction, investigate it like an acute hemolytic reaction
claims.quote: Clinically, febrile reactions consist of a temperature increase of ≥ 1° C, chills, and sometimes headache and back pain. Simultaneous symptoms of allergic reactions are common. Because fever and chills also herald a severe hemolytic transfusion reaction, all febrile reactions must be investigated as for acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, as with any transfusion reaction.

claims.text: Febrile reaction treatment: acetaminophen and, if needed, diphenhydramine; premedicate before future transfusions; after more than one febrile reaction, use leukoreduced products
claims.quote: Most febrile reactions are treated successfully with acetaminophen and, if necessary, diphenhydramine. Patients should also be treated (eg, with acetaminophen) before future transfusions. If a recipient has experienced more than one febrile reaction, special leukoreduction filters are used during future transfusions; most hospitals use previously stored, leukoreduced (WBC-depleted RBCs) blood components.

claims.text: Acute hemolytic reaction (AHTR) cause: most often ABO incompatibility, usually from a mislabeled pretransfusion sample or not matching the patient to the unit right before transfusion
claims.quote: ABO incompatibility is the most common cause of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. Antibodies against blood group antigens other than ABO can also cause AHTR. Mislabeling the recipient’s pretransfusion sample at collection and failing to match the intended recipient with the blood product immediately before transfusion are the usual causes.

claims.text: AHTR presentation: usually within 1 hour of starting, abrupt; dyspnea, fever, chills, facial flushing, severe pain (especially lumbar), and possibly shock
claims.quote: An acute phase usually develops within 1 hour of initiation of transfusion, but it may occur later during the transfusion or immediately afterward. Onset is usually abrupt. The patient may complain of discomfort and anxiety. Dyspnea, fever, chills, facial flushing, and severe pain may occur, especially in the lumbar area. Shock may develop, causing a rapid, feeble pulse; cold, clammy skin; low blood pressure; and nausea and vomiting.

claims.text: AHTR under general anesthesia: may show only as hypotension, uncontrollable bleeding from DIC, or dark urine
claims.quote: If AHTR occurs while the patient is under general anesthesia, the only symptom may be hypotension, uncontrollable bleeding from incision sites and mucous membranes caused by an associated DIC, or dark urine that reflects hemoglobinuria.

claims.text: AHTR workup: first recheck the labels on the sample and the patient; confirm with a positive direct antiglobulin test plus urine hemoglobin, LDH, bilirubin and haptoglobin (very low)
claims.quote: If AHTR is suspected, one of the first steps is to recheck the identification labels on the sample and patient. Diagnosis is confirmed by a positive direct antiglobulin test, eluting the antibody attached to the donor red cells to confirm the cause, and measuring urinary hemoglobin, serum lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin, and haptoglobin. Intravascular hemolysis produces free hemoglobin in the plasma and urine; haptoglobin levels are very low.

claims.text: AHTR treatment: stop the transfusion; IV 0.9% saline to keep urine output at 100 mL/hour for 24 hours, plus furosemide 40 to 80 mg IV initially
claims.quote: If AHTR is suspected, the transfusion should be stopped and supportive treatment begun. The goal of initial therapy is to achieve and maintain adequate blood pressure and renal blood flow with IV 0.9% saline and furosemide. IV saline is given to maintain urine output of 100 mL/hour for 24 hours. The initial IV furosemide dose is 40 to 80 mg (1 to 2 mg/kg in children), with later doses adjusted to maintain a urinary flow of > 100 mL/hour during the first day.

claims.text: Pressors in AHTR: avoid those that reduce renal blood flow (epinephrine, norepinephrine, high-dose dopamine); if one is needed, usually dopamine 2 to 5 mcg/kg/minute IV
claims.quote: Pharmacologic treatment of hypotension must be done cautiously. Pressor medications that decrease renal blood flow (eg, epinephrine, norepinephrine, high-dose dopamine) are contraindicated. If a pressor medication is necessary, dopamine 2 to 5 mcg/kg/minute IV is usually used.

claims.text: No diuretic response within about 2 to 3 hours: may mean acute tubular necrosis; consult nephrology early, as early dialysis may help
claims.quote: A nephrologist should be consulted as early as possible, particularly if no diuretic response occurs within approximately 2 to 3 hours after initiating therapy, which may indicate acute tubular necrosis. Further fluid and diuretic therapy may be contraindicated, and early dialysis may be helpful.

claims.text: Delayed hemolytic reaction: usually 1 to 4 weeks after; usually mild, with a falling hematocrit, slight rise in LDH and bilirubin, and a positive direct antiglobulin test; the clue may be an unexplained Hb drop to the pretransfusion level 1 to 2 weeks later
claims.quote: Occasionally, a patient who has been sensitized to an RBC antigen has very low antibody levels and negative pretransfusion tests. After transfusion with RBCs bearing this antigen, a primary or anamnestic response may result (usually in 1 to 4 weeks) and cause a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction. A delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction usually does not manifest as dramatically as acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. Patients may be asymptomatic or have a slight fever. Rarely, severe symptoms (eg, fever, chills, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal or flank pain) occur. Usually, only destruction of the transfused RBCs (with the antigen) occurs, resulting in a falling hematocrit and a slight rise in lactate dehydrogenase and bilirubin and a positive direct antiglobulin test. Because delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction is usually mild and self-limited, it is often unidentified, and the clinical clue may be an unexplained drop in hemoglobin to the pretransfusion level occurring 1 to 2 weeks posttransfusion.

claims.text: Allergic reaction: stop the transfusion; an antihistamine usually controls mild urticaria and itching and the transfusion may resume; moderate (generalized urticaria or mild bronchospasm) also needs hydrocortisone 100 to 200 mg IV; anaphylaxis needs epinephrine 0.5 mL of 1:1000 subcutaneously and IV saline
claims.quote: If an allergic reaction occurs, the transfusion is stopped. An antihistamine usually controls mild urticaria and itching, and transfusion may be resumed. However, a moderate allergic reaction (generalized urticaria or mild bronchospasm) also requires hydrocortisone (100 to 200 mg IV), and a severe anaphylactic reaction requires additional treatment with epinephrine 0.5 mL of 1:1000 solution subcutaneously and 0.9% saline IV along with investigation by the blood bank.

claims.text: History of allergic reactions: an antihistamine just before or at the start (e.g., diphenhydramine 50 mg orally or IV); never mix medications with the blood
claims.quote: In a patient with a history of allergies or an allergic transfusion reaction, an antihistamine may be given prophylactically just before or at the beginning of the transfusion (eg, diphenhydramine 50 mg orally or IV). NOTE: Medications must never be mixed with the blood.

claims.text: Severe IgA deficiency: washed RBCs, washed platelets, or plasma from an IgA-deficient donor
claims.quote: Patients with severe IgA deficiency require transfusion of washed RBCs, washed platelets, or plasma from an IgA-deficient donor.

claims.text: TACO prevention: infuse RBCs slowly and watch; at signs of heart failure, stop the transfusion and treat the heart failure
claims.quote: RBCs should be infused slowly. The patient should be observed and, if signs of heart failure occur, the transfusion should be stopped and treatment for heart failure begun.

claims.text: TACO treatment: typically a diuretic such as furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV; high-risk patients (heart failure, severe renal insufficiency) get a diuretic prophylactically
claims.quote: Typical treatment is with a diuretic such as furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV. Occasionally, patients requiring a higher volume of plasma infusion to reverse a warfarin overdose may be given a low dose of furosemide simultaneously; however, prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is the first choice for such patients. Patients at high risk of TACO (eg, those with heart failure or severe renal insufficiency) are treated prophylactically with a diuretic.

claims.text: TRALI: donor anti-HLA and/or antigranulocyte antibodies cause noncardiogenic pulmonary edema; supportive care, avoid diuretics, and report it to the blood bank
claims.quote: Anti-HLA and/or antigranulocyte antibodies in donor plasma agglutinate and degranulate recipient granulocytes within the lung, causing TRALI. Acute respiratory symptoms develop, and chest radiographs have a characteristic pattern of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. General supportive therapy typically leads to recovery without long-lasting sequelae. Diuretics should be avoided. Cases should be reported to the hospital transfusion medicine service or blood bank.

claims.text: Transfusion GVHD: > 90% mortality with no specific treatment, so it is prevented by irradiating cellular products (RBCs and platelets)
claims.quote: GVHD has > 90% mortality because no specific treatment is available. Prevention of GVHD is with irradiation (to damage DNA of the donor lymphocytes) of transfused cellular blood products (RBCs and platelets).

claims.text: Irradiate when: the recipient is immunocompromised, the donor is a first-degree relative, or HLA-matched components are given; glucocorticoids or other immunosuppressants alone are not an indication
claims.quote: When the recipient is immunocompromised (eg, patients with congenital immune deficiency syndromes, hematologic cancers, or hematopoietic stem cell transplants; neonates) When donor blood is obtained from a first-degree relative (because the donor is homozygous and the recipient is heterozygous for the HLA antigens, the recipient does not reject donor lymphocytes, which in turn attack the recipient's other HLA haplotype bearing all cells, including the bone marrow, causing severe aplastic anemia, and often death) When HLA-matched components, excluding stem cells, are transfused (because the recipient is immunocompromised and cannot reject donor lymphocytes, which would attack mismatched HLA antigens on all tissues) Treatment with glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressants, including those used for solid organ transplantation, is not an indication for blood irradiation.
